name: tools/agentspec
body_head:
===== tools/agentspec/README.md =====
# agentspec

The portable, vendor-neutral **agent-workflow SPEC**, the shared **observation envelope**, the
**dispatch-safety pure core**, and a **hermetic regression-eval registry**.

Stdlib-only, zero runtime dependencies, no I/O on the dispatch path, no wall clock, no entropy.

## Why this package exists

**It is the SINGLE HOME for dispatch safety.** Two independent plans were building the same
argv guard, the same completion oracle and the same progress-stream rejection twice. Any runtime
or vendor adapter now *consumes* these functions; it must not reimplement them.

**The spec is the SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH.** A runtime does not invent its own dialect: it loads a
`Workflow`, validates it with `validate_workflow`, and translates it to whatever its vendor rail
needs. That is the mitigation the "second orchestration runtime" decision rests on — without one
shared spec, two runtimes diverge into rival dialects.

## Layout

| module | what it owns |
|---|---|
| `spec.py` | frozen declarative types: `WorkUnit`, `FanOut`, `Barrier`, `Pipeline`, `Workflow`, `ReceiptSpec` |
| `validate.py` | the closed 28-id violation set over a `Workflow` |
| `envelope.py` | `status` / `summary` / `next_actions` / `artifacts` + the error path's three recovery fields |
| `taxonomy.py` | the closed failure vocabulary every lane matches on (+ `family` for polic

prior_does: The portable, vendor-neutral agent-workflow SPEC + shared observation envelope + dispatch-safety pure core + hermetic regression-eval registry. Stdlib-only, no I/O on the dispatch path, no wall clock, no entropy.

name: tools/agentrail
body_head:
===== tools/agentrail/README.md =====
# agentrail

A **config-driven multi-rail agent dispatch shell** over [`agentspec`](../agentspec).

Adding an agent CLI is a row in [`agentrail/rails.toml`](agentrail/rails.toml) — not new Python.
agentrail is the *consumer* of agentspec and the proof that the spec is vendor-neutral: five
rails from four vendors ride the same core with zero per-vendor code.

```console
$ agentrail rails
$ agentrail resolve codex
$ agentrail plan  codex --unit-id u1 --prompt-file ./prompt.txt
$ agentrail run   codex --unit-id u1 --prompt-file ./prompt.txt --receipt-path ./r.txt
$ agentrail deploy                     # writes ~/.local/bin/agentrail.cmd, under a guard
```

Every command prints one JSON object carrying agentspec's four mandated envelope fields —
`status`, `summary`, `next_actions`, `artifacts` — plus `error{code, root_cause,
retry_instruction, stop_condition}` on a failure and a `terminal` marker always. One shape on
the success path and the failure path; **"error-only output without next steps" is a named
anti-pattern and there is no code path here that produces it.**

---

## The reuse boundary

This is the whole point of the package, so it is stated precisely and **gated mechanically**.

| Concern | Owner | agentrail's part |
|---|---|---|
| Completion AND-gate (six clauses) | `agentspec.oracle.judge` | calls it |
| Closed failure taxonomy

name: tools/fanout-schema
body_head:
===== tools/fanout-schema/README.md =====
# Fan-out schema design guide

`StructuredOutput` is the fan-in surface of every Claude Code Workflow in this workspace. It
fails **22.7% of the time**, and the failures are ours: our own schemas rejecting our own
agents' work. This directory holds the measurement, the rules it produced, and a module that
makes the dominant failure unrepresentable.

Run the tests: `node --test tools/fanout-schema/`
Lint the schemas you already have: import `lintSource` (see *Auditing what you already wrote*).

---

## 1. What was measured

Scan of **11,693 transcripts / 10.65 GB** under `~/.claude/projects`, joined to the **637
schema literals** declared across **435 workflow scripts** in `*/workflows/scripts/*.js`.

| | calls | errors | rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| StructuredOutput, all | 3,735 | 849 | **22.7%** |

The distilled corpus reports 3,694 / 846 / 22.9% from an independent implementation. Two
mechanically different miners agreeing within 1.1% is the reason these numbers are quoted as
fact rather than estimate.

### Failure taxonomy (n = 849)

| class | n | share |
|---|---|---|
| missing required property | 616 | 72.6% |
| unparseable JSON | 176 | 20.7% |
| `additionalProperties: false` rejection | 30 | 3.5% |
| wrong type | 14 | 1.6% |
| other / non-schema | 13 | 1.5% |
| enum mismatch | 0 | 0% |
| too deep / too many items / too long | 0 | 0
prior_evidence: tools/fanout-schema/README.md: 'It fails 22.7% of the time, and the failures are ours.' Corroborated by _wfcat_exec.json: 169 of 329 executed workflows carry a schema: fan-in.

name: tools/repomap
body_head:
===== tools/repomap/README.md =====
# `tools/repomap` — the fan-out grounding pack

`rules/common/fan-out-contract.md` §A11 prescribes injecting a **shared grounding
pack** into every fan-out:

> 16/25 agents read the same `codex_monitor.py`; 13/25 the same
> `codex-monitor.md`; one agent re-read `hub.py` **×22**. One grounding agent
> producing a pinned digest removes an estimated 60-90 tool calls in a single
> 39-agent workflow.

Nothing in this repository generated one. This is that generator: a
deterministic, stdlib-only repo map that ranks the most central files and
symbols and emits a digest sized to a token budget.

No embeddings. No vector store. No model call. Same tree in, same bytes out.

---

## Use it

```bash
# a ~900-token pack for a fan-out prompt
python tools/repomap/repo_map.py --budget 900 --out pack.md

# steer it at the area a wave is about to touch
python tools/repomap/repo_map.py --budget 900 \
    --focus tools/monitorcore/monitorcore/hub.py --mention poll_once

# drop vendored/duplicated trees that add bulk but no structure
python tools/repomap/repo_map.py --budget 900 \
    --exclude '.agents/skills/**' --exclude 'tools/crcp/vendor_src/**'

# machine-readable (ranks + digest together)
python tools/repomap/repo_map.py --budget 900 --json
```

| flag | effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--root PATH` | repository root (default `.`) |
| `--budget N` | token budget
prior_evidence: tools/repomap/README.md quotes the A11 measurement (16/25 agents re-read the same file; one agent x22). Rule A11 warns its path is repo-relative -> pass the ABSOLUTE form.
prior_does: PageRank-over-symbol-references grounding-pack generator, sized to a token budget. The mechanised form of fan-out-contract A11 (inject a shared grounding pack).
prior_maintenance: versioned on real main; deployment state to live tree NOT audited here

A **standalone CLI + importable Python module** that routes a metaswarm

===== tools/mutation-gate/README.md =====
# TG-2 — diff-scoped mutation gate

**Coverage says a line *ran*. Mutation says a test would *notice* if that line broke.**

A line at 100% coverage can still be unasserted: the motivating scar is a
`DEFAULT_MIN_BYTES` default that every test passed *explicitly*, so mutating the
constant changed nothing any test observed — 100% coverage, zero protection.

This gate perturbs the source of the files a diff touched and fails when any
**mutant survives** (i.e. the whole test suite still passes with the code
subtly broken), naming the surviving mutant and the weak suite that let it live.

- **Diff-scoped** (the cost control): it mutates only the files in
  `git diff --name-only <base>...HEAD` — never the whole tree.
- **Self-contained**: stdlib + one pinned mutation tool. Nothing here touches the

===== tools/ese-gate/README.md =====
# ESE Gate — Ensemble Semantic Entropy Escalation Gate

A standalone Python CLI that quantifies cross-model disagreement in a
multi-model code-generation council (Claude / Codex / Gemini) and emits a
deterministic routing decision:

```
low entropy  (models agree)     → escalate=false → accept cheaply
high entropy (models disagree)  → escalate=true  → deep-review lane
```

Disagreement is measured on **execution-equivalence** — do the candidates
behave identically when run against your test suite? — not on self-reported
confidence scores.  This gives an external, falsifiable signal.

---

## How It Works

1. **Receive** N candidate patches (one per council model) via a JSON manifest.
2. **Isolate** — copy the workdir to a fresh temp directory per candidate.
3. **Apply** — unified diff (`patch -p1`) or files-map (`{"path": "content"}`).
4. **Execute** — run `test_cmd`; capture exit code + stdout/stderr.
5. **Fingerprint** — hash (exit\_code, sorted test pass/fail ids) into a
   16-hex behaviour signature.  Two candidates are *execution-equivalent* iff
   their signature matches.
6. **Cluster** candidates by signature.
7. **Entropy** — normalised Shannon entropy over cluster-size distribution:

   ```
   H = -Σ p_i * log(p_i) / log(N)   ∈ [0, 1]
   ```

   `H = 0` → all models agree; `H = 1` → every model produced a distinct
   behaviour.

8.

===== tools/detector-self-test/README.md =====
# TG-1 · detector self-test

A **both-states fixture gate** for the estate's harness detectors, hooks, and
gates. It mechanizes the single-signal-verification §3b rule ("the both-states
test") and is mutation-testing applied to the harness's own instruments.

## The problem it closes

A *detector* is any check that is supposed to **FIRE** on a broken input and stay
**SILENT** on a fixed one — a linter rule, a security guard, a validator, a hook
predicate, a CI grep. Two silent failure modes routinely ship green:

- **silent-in-both** — the detector never fires, so it catches nothing. Its
  silence on real input reads as "clean". (Ledger: a `codex exec` probe that
  printed no error in the broken state *or* the fixed state — it measured nothing.)
- **firing-in-both** — the detector always fires, so its signal is noise.

100% line coverage does **not** catch either: coverage proves a line *ran*, never
that the detector would *fire when it should and stay quiet when it shouldn't*.
This gate does, by running each detector against a known-broken **and** a
known-fixed fixture and asserting the two disagree in the right direction.

## Fixture layout

Each detector under test is a directory holding a `detector.py` plus a
`broken/` + `fixed/` fixture pair:

```
<root>/<name>/
    detector.py       # def detect(target: Path) -> object   (tr

`mine.py` previously reported `hooks: {}` across the whole corpus and published

# event-ledger — the N2 keystone (anti-echo-chamber memory)

**Deployed at:** `~/.claude/hooks/event-ledger/` (this is the versioned copy — keep in sync).

The root fix for the post-compaction **echo-chamber** + repetitive actions: an append-only,
failure-aware, per-project **typed event ledger** that hooks write continuously, and that
**recovery replays as ground truth** instead of trusting a lossy self-summary.

Compaction keeps *what happened* and destroys *why* (decisions/failures/rationale). The

===== tools/memory-bench/README.md =====
# memory-bench — basic-memory recall regression suite

Deep-research item **#5** (modus-operandi scan, 2026-06-15). Converts "memory
feels useful" into a single measured pass-rate by probing whether **basic-memory
actually recalls correctly** across sessions. Based on LongMemEval
(arXiv:2410.10813) + LoCoMo-style probes.

## What it measures

Five recall ability-classes, scored with a deterministic substring/abstention
scorer (NO LLM-as-judge — that would be a same-context placebo):

| Class | What it tests |
|---|---|
| information-extraction | recall a fact stated in an earlier note |
| multi-session-temporal | fact spans multiple notes / dates |
| knowledge-update | a later note overrides an earlier one → recall the CURRENT value |
| abstention | asked about something never stored → correct answer is "not found" |
| contradiction | conflicting notes → resolve correctly |

## Baseline (first run, 2026-06-15) — `results.json`

**Overall: 13/16 = 81.25%.** Per-class: abstention 3/3, knowledge-update 3/3,
information-extraction 4/5, multi-session-temporal 2/3, **contradiction 1/2**.
The weak spots (contradiction, temporal) are the expected hard cases for flat
top-k semantic recall — this is the number to beat after any future memory change.

## Run it

```bash
python tools/memory-bench/memory_bench.py
```

Uses a **scratch** basic-memory

===== tools/d001-dual-write/README.md =====
# `d001_apply.py` — filter-safe D-001 dual-write applier

`.agents/skills/` is the authoritative skill root; `skills/` is a compatibility
projection (`AGENTS.md`). When a change lands a skill under `skills/<NAME>/`
only, the fix is to mirror the **same blobs** onto `.agents/skills/<NAME>/`.

This tool does that with **plumbing only**. It never creates a second working
tree, never restores the whole index, and never round-trips a file through a
content filter. Protected paths are therefore never opened for write: their
bytes *and* their mtime are unchanged by a full run.

## Why the obvious procedure is unsafe here

This repository encrypts `tools/mcp/*/accounts.json` with git-crypt
(`.gitattributes`). Every materialising git operation writes files through that
filter's *smudge* side. If the filter has been reduced to an identity
passthrough — `smudge = cat`, `clean = cat`, `required = false` in the **shared**
`.git/config`, a state this repository was measurably in — then:

1. **The damage lands on the first command.** A second working tree of the same
   repository inherits the shared config, so creating one writes the STORED
   (encrypted) bytes into it for every protected path, including paths the
   procedure never intended to touch. Narrowing a *later* per-file step does not
   help: the tree is already corrupt before that step
